newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - European chemicals desperate to be special.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - European chemicals desperate to be special.

text.p: The swoop this month by Britain's Imperial Chemical Industries Plc on 4.9 billion pounds ($8 billion) of Unilever Plc businesses put it at the head of a scramble by Europe's chemical industry for the profitable high ground of specialisation.

ICI hopes the acquisitions, offset by three billion pounds of disposals, will transport it at a stroke from the highly cyclical, low margin and overcrowded world of basic chemicals to the sunny uplands of less volatile and high margin products aimed at consumers, industry and agriculture.

Analysts said ICI's move into starches, adhesives, food flavourings and detergents had stolen a march on many of its European rivals, all of whom are anxious about the rising tide of competition in basic chemicals from the booming Asian economies and the Middle East, where raw materials are cheap.
"The industry has really got the blues at the moment," said Williams de Broe analyst Peter Cartwright. "It is convinced that overcapacity is here to stay."
BULK CHEMICALS OUT OF FASHION

ICI's transformation, which will leave British basic chemical production almost exclusively in the hands of oil giants Royal Dutch/Shell and British Petroleum Plc, is the latest in a series of moves away from bulk production across Europe.

An official of the European Chemical Industry Council, CEFIC, who asked not to be named, said: "Everybody thinks they should move into speciality chemicals, like pharmaceuticals, partly because it doesn't have the smell of bulk chemicals and commodities. Commodities stink -- it's a fashion."

Oversupply and tumbling prices in key areas of bulk chemicals like polyester, tioxide and PVC have created the bad odour. Many blame rises in capacity by Asian producers, some of whom are willing to sustain years of start-up losses to get established.

Juergen Dormann, chairman of the world's biggest chemicals company Hoechst AG, painted an almost apocalyptic picture of prospects for European economies, on which the chemical industry is so dependent, at a forum last year.

Dormann said Europe was "losing global market shares, losing ground in key technologies, such as information technology and biotechnology, and as a consequence venture capital and direct investment are increasingly being routed to other continents and regions."
He added that "our vitality is fading and sustainability is not within reach."
GERMANS LEAD MOVE TO RESTRUCTURE
Hoechst and its two German peers BASF AG and Bayer AG -- the world's top three chemical companies in terms of sales -- led the dash for restructuring before ICI made its move.

Last year Dormann's company took advantage of the premium on specialties to sell its specialty business to Switzerland's Clariant AG. At its results presentation this month, management stressed that Hoechst's focus would be on the life sciences, notably its underperforming drugs operation Hoechst Marion Roussel, and agricultural chemicals. Bayer also set out plans last year to increase its focus on healthcare, agro-chemicals, polymers and specialites, while BASF has set up major joint ventures to produce polyethylene, used in plastic bags, containers and wiring, and polypropylene. It hopes to smooth out some of the worst peaks and troughs of bulk chemical cycles by pooling marketing and technology.
In France Rhone Poulenc SA has set increasing store on its drugs business, Rhone Poulenc Rorer Inc.
Companies could well be making the right moves in terms of survival. Williams de Broe's Cartwright said the Unilever acquisition "was like manna from heaven for ICI -- it was a lifeline."
FASHION MAY SWING BACK

Analysts said the outlook for basic chemicals continued to look shaky. Some analysts expect a rise in capacity in areas like ethylene, polyethylene, polyester and styrene to come on stream this year and next, and Salomon Brothers said earlier this year that it was wary about prospects for companies with large petrochemical exposure, notably BASF and Belgium's Solvay SA.
But Salomon said that ultimately "it is the transport costs for commodity chemicals which will provide some protection for the producers which remain."
CEFIC too believes the fashion will swing back towards bulk chemicals as specialty producers start to wonder where their raw materials will come from.
Keith Wey, senior economist at Britain's Chemical Industries Association, said the industry had to focus on being globally competitive, both by investing in research and cutting overheads.
"It is still possible to make money out of bulk products if you get your operations right. And that means getting your costs right," Wey said. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
